source.title: On Implicit Filter Level Sparsity in Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Dushyant Mehta; K. Kim; Christian Theobalt

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and supplementary document. Some table columns are flattened, but the main batch-size tables remain interpretable.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally varies optimizer, regularization, and batch size and reports training and held-out results, but its main outcome is implicit filter sparsity rather than the claim’s generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The study reports test errors and training losses while varying optimizer, regularizer, and batch size. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolution-versus-fully-connected generalization, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removing memorized examples. Its sparsity and selectivity measurements are not direct measures of the train-test gap.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with momentum SGD using held-out classification errors, bearing on V4. Its batch-size sweeps hold training iterations constant and adjust epochs, so they do not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors attribute emergent filter sparsity to disproportionate regularization relative to task gradients, compounded by Adam's selective features and the interaction of L2 with adaptive updates. They conclude that common training choices control capacity–accuracy tradeoffs and can enable CNN speedups without explicit sparsification.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures implicit filter sparsity and reports test errors while varying optimizer, regularizer, and batch size; it does not reproduce the claim’s random-label memorization or generalization-gap experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer, regularizer type and strength, mini-batch size, dataset/task difficulty, network capacity, and learning-rate scaling for BatchNorm parameters affect reported sparsity; batch size also changes reported held-out errors.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive updates and regularization induce filter sparsity, with its extent depending on feature selectivity, batch size, task difficulty, and network capacity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam with regularization can implicitly remove substantial CNN capacity through filter sparsification.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch-size sweeps show mixed held-out error trends while holding optimizer updates constant and changing epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed number of updates, changing batch size alters accuracy and sparsity in a dataset-dependent way.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (venue as supplied)
record.problems: The study's main outcome is filter sparsity, not the train-test gap. CIFAR results are averaged over 3 runs, TinyImageNet over 2, and ImageNet over 1; no uncertainty intervals are reported. Some table content is flattened in the supplied text, limiting reliable optimizer-specific value attribution. Batch-size comparisons keep iterations the same, and the ImageNet description says epochs are adjusted with batch size, so they do not directly test the fixed-epoch condition in V5.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every optimizer-by-regularizer setting in Table 1 because the flattened table layout does not reliably assign the rendered values. Layerwise sparsity and post-pruning errors in Tables 2, 7–10, plus supplemental tables, are omitted because they measure pruning/sparsity outcomes rather than a claim version's named generalization behavior.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Widening beyond the interpolation threshold with zero training error; the limited capacity comparison does not establish this regime.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.

Language benchmarks, systematic learning-rate and schedule tuning, broad hyperparameter tuning, and switching from Adam to SGD. Decoupled weight decay is tested, but recovery from an established Adam disadvantage is not demonstrated.
Fixed-epoch batch-size penalties and their removal by adapted training recipes. The reported sweeps instead keep iterations constant.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and comparing retraining with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1's optimizer blocks can be identified by cross-checking the explicitly labeled layerwise tables. Its zeros are sparsity values, not losses. Remaining optimizer configurations and pruning comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out. The condition-specific V4 challenges do not establish that adaptive optimizers generally outperform SGD. CIFAR results average three runs and TinyImageNet two; no uncertainty intervals establish the significance of the smaller differences.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error and test error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization comparisons.

No language benchmarks; no broad hyperparameter tuning comparison; no switching from Adam to SGD or decoupled weight decay assessment. The optimizer comparisons focus on sparsity and selected test-error configurations.
No fixed-epoch comparison of large and small batches; batch-size comparisons are arranged to keep training iterations the same. No language models.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
